r: The applied work is physically flying aerobatic and glider maneuvers with precision, executing timed and accuracy events for International Aerobatic Club collegiate competition. These map to O*NET activities centered on operating vehicles and controlling machines in real time — categories task-exposure research consistently places among the least automatable, alongside manual and physical work strongly negatively associated with exposure. Generating a maneuver sequence on paper is trivial for a model; performing a competition-grade snap roll under g-load in an actual airframe is not a task any system executes for the student. Embodiment is the binding constraint: the competence is psychomotor airmanship cultivated in the cockpit under real aerodynamic and physiological stress. Autoflight exists and is irrelevant to a pilot demonstrating hand-flown aerobatic accuracy. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire this embodied skill is wholly intact; there is no route by which AI performs the flying itself.

By 2031, autonomy and flight-management systems will be more capable, and simulation may support more pre-flight rehearsal of aerobatic sequences. None of that reaches the course's core: developing a human pilot's real-time psychomotor control and spatial judgment during high-energy maneuvering. Verification burden here is definitional and safety-critical — an aerobatic error is immediate and physically dangerous, exactly the adversarial, non-obvious-failure condition the jagged-frontier evidence shows keeps human competence necessary. Diffusion of capable autonomy into hand-flown collegiate aerobatic training is essentially nil on this horizon, and adoption of AI in physical skill acquisition lags capability broadly. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and by the physical nature of the demonstrated competence. The rating stays Low; nothing in the capability trajectory substitutes for a student personally learning to fly precision aerobatics.

By 2036 highly automated flight will be materially more capable, and one can imagine autonomous systems flying aerobatic profiles. Even so, the specific competence this lab builds — a human athlete-pilot's embodied control, g-tolerance, and real-time precision under competition conditions — is not a task AI executes on the student's behalf; embodiment is the entire point. The most plausible decade-scale change is in the tools that support training and analysis, not in whether learning to fly aerobatics requires doing it. Task-exposure frameworks keep real-time vehicle operation and physical skill among the most durable human categories, and no model performs the psychomotor act for the learner. The rating holds Low; the honest caveat concerns the broader aviation labor market, not the instrumental necessity of embodied aerobatic training, which remains intact under any credible central case.
AES 0345.d: The Aerobatic and Glider Course is a continuation of AES 2350 further preparing the students for participation in the International Aerobatic Club (IAC) Collegiate Program national team and individual collegiate events. Aerobatic flight maneuvers, precision, accuracy and timed events are learned. Required for all students who are members of the MSU Denver Aerobatic and Glider Team.

r: The course teaches aviation and aerospace management: operations, regulatory compliance, strategic planning, safety and risk management, and logistics for airports, airlines, spaceports, and air traffic systems. The applied tasks — drafting strategy, synthesizing regulations, structuring risk analyses, producing management reports — are white-collar activities that observed-usage data shows are a prominent and growing share of AI use, and GDPval indicates models approach but remain below expert parity on real occupational deliverables. There is no licensure or accreditation lock on this managerial content. At 24 months the instrumental need is only modestly eroded: AI can draft a compliance summary or a risk matrix, but management judgment — allocating resources, owning safety accountability, and deciding under regulatory constraint — still rests with a trained human. Diffusion also lags capability, with a minority of firms yet using AI. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will competently draft strategic plans, compile regulatory analyses, and generate the reporting and logistics artifacts this course's knowledge produces, materially reducing the routine execution. The instrumental case erodes toward specifying, directing, and verifying AI-generated management work rather than composing it, and absent any institutional mandate nothing caps that erosion. Management analysis sits among the more exposed office-and-business categories in the evidence base, which pushes the rating up. The residual human role — accountable decision-making, contextual judgment about safety-critical trade-offs, stakeholder coordination — is real but does not by itself hold the course at Low. The rating rises to High: the applied tasks are substantially AI-performable and, with no licensure lock, little structural friction resists that shift within a catalog cycle.

A decade out, the central case has AI handling most of the analytical and documentary work of aviation management — regulatory synthesis, strategic drafting, resource optimization, and risk reporting — with the human role concentrated in accountable judgment and negotiation. The instrumental rationale for learning to produce these managerial artifacts is substantially eroded, and no accreditation or licensure structure protects the course. The rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty is how much accountable decision authority and safety ownership remain reserved to trained managers versus delegated to AI-assisted systems; diffusion and organizational inertia could slow the transition. But on the rating's own question — whether AI competently performs the work tasks this knowledge is applied to — the answer trends strongly yes, and there is no institutional brake to hold it lower.
AES 1010.d: Students are introduced to a comprehensive exploration of the principles, practices, and challenges of aviation and aerospace management. Students will examine the operations, regulations, and strategic planning involved in managing complex aviation and aerospace systems, including airports, airlines, spaceports, and air traffic control. The course covers essential management areas such as safety and risk management, aerospace mission logistics, regulatory compliance, and sustainability within the aviation and aerospace sectors.

r: This is the introductory knowledge course on unmanned aircraft systems: operational familiarity with vehicles, flight and ground control processes, FAA regulations, mission operations, and human-factors and ethical considerations — distinct from the embodied flight-and-control lab that follows. The applied tasks are informational and analytical: interpreting UAS regulations, describing mission-planning logic, and reasoning about applications. Observed-usage data shows such office and knowledge tasks are heavily represented in AI use, and models handle regulatory summary and conceptual explanation competently. No licensure gates the course credit itself. At 24 months the instrumental need is partly eroded — AI can explain UAS regulation and operations on demand — but the course still grounds the conceptual vocabulary a student applies in later applied coursework, and adoption remains uneven across firms. Rating Medium, reflecting a knowledge course rather than an embodied one.

By 2031, AI will fluently deliver, tutor, and update UAS operational and regulatory knowledge, and capability trends (task-time-horizon doubling every several months) suggest the informational core of this survey is increasingly AI-supplied. The instrumental rationale for a student to internalize this material as a course erodes toward using AI to retrieve and apply it, with source-verification the durable residue. There is no accreditation or licensure lock to cap that erosion at the course level. UAS knowledge tasks — regulatory interpretation, mission-concept reasoning — are the exposed, information-centric kind the evidence flags as positively associated with exposure. The rating rises to High, tempered only by the observation that operational familiarity still supports safe field practice a graduate must demonstrate elsewhere.

A decade out, AI will be an authoritative and interactive source on UAS operations, regulation, and mission design, and the pure knowledge-transmission function of this introductory course is largely eroded. The human residue — ethical judgment and safety accountability in real operations — is real but is exercised in the applied field courses, not in this survey. With no institutional lock protecting the course, the rating holds High. The honest uncertainty is pedagogical and regulatory: how UAS training is structured once AI supplies the operational knowledge, and how fast the FAA's own certification expectations evolve. But on the instrumental question, the informational tasks this course teaches are among the more automatable, and nothing structural holds the rating lower in the central case.
AES 1040.d: This course gives the student pursuing aviation science an operational knowledge of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). This includes small, medium, and large aviation vehicles (AV), flight and ground control processes, FAA regulations, UAS applications, mission operations, ethical and human factors concerns, and future considerations.

r: This general-studies science course introduces space systems and operations, with a hands-on arc: students design, build, and fly a near-space payload and analyze the returned data. The applied tasks blend scientific reasoning — which task-exposure research places among the least exposed categories — with a physical build-and-fly component and quantitative data analysis that is more automatable. The binding constraint is institutional: the course carries a GT-Pathways Natural and Physical Sciences designation, a statutory general-education transfer element, which mandates its transferable existence regardless of tool capability. At 24 months the instrumental need is not eroded; AI can explain orbital mechanics or process telemetry, but the course develops the student's own scientific literacy and includes embodied payload construction. Foundational scientific reasoning and the transfer mandate hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will fluently explain space-systems concepts and can assist the data-analysis portion of the payload project, weakening the rationale for students to perform that analysis unaided. The instrumental case shifts toward conceptual understanding and the hands-on experimental competence, and toward critically evaluating AI-generated scientific claims. The GT-Pathways Natural Sciences designation caps the erosion: the course stays locked in the statewide general-education core across a catalog cycle. Science and critical-thinking skills remain negatively associated with exposure, which resists a High. The rating rises to Medium: the quantitative and explanatory tasks are increasingly AI-deliverable, but the transfer mandate and the embodied experimental core keep the course instrumentally necessary through this horizon.

A decade out, AI will be a capable explainer of space science and could handle most routine analysis of payload data, substantially eroding the information-and-computation rationale. But the general-education Natural and Physical Sciences requirement persists in the central case absent statewide policy change, and the hands-on design-build-fly experience develops competence AI does not supply to the learner. The rating holds Medium, capped by the GT-Pathways lock from either rising to High or falling to Low. The uncertainty is pedagogical — how a lab-inflected science course is taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI — not whether the transfer mandate and its scientific-literacy aim remain, which in the central case they do.
AES 1050.d: Students are introduced to space systems to provide a basic understanding of space operations and associated scientific principles of space exploration. Abstract concepts are translated to a tangible application through the design, construction, flight, and subsequent analysis of data returned from a working near-space payload. Current space missions are also discussed in the context of the space environment and the broader impact on society.

r: Private Pilot Ground is the aeronautical-knowledge substrate for the flight program: aircraft operation and performance, aerodynamics, federal aviation regulations, weather theory, flight physiology, and air navigation by pilotage, dead reckoning, and radio aids. The applied tasks — regulatory interpretation, navigation computation, weather reasoning — are digital and increasingly AI-exposed, and flight-planning software already automates much of the arithmetic. But this course is critical foundational scaffolding for the entire certificated-pilot sequence; nearly every downstream flight and instrument course lists it as prerequisite, and a pilot must hold this knowledge to operate safely. At 24 months the instrumental need is not eroded despite high task-exposure: a model can compute a navigation log, but the course exists so students can reason aeronautically in the cockpit and in later coursework. Foundational role holds the rating at Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently perform every computation and much of the regulatory and weather interpretation this course teaches, sharpening the question of why students learn it themselves. The instrumental case shifts from execution to the conceptual fluency a pilot needs to fly and to supervise automated flight-planning tools — a real change, but foundational scaffolding caps the erosion. Because the entire downstream flight curriculum depends on this substrate, the rating is held at Medium rather than rising to High: a student cannot meaningfully build instrument, dispatch, or ATC knowledge without it. The jagged-frontier caution applies — a plausible-looking but wrong nav or weather answer is dangerous in flight — reinforcing the need for the human to hold the knowledge, not merely to prompt for it.

A decade out, AI competently executes flight planning, regulatory lookup, and weather interpretation, and the do-it-by-hand rationale is largely eroded. Yet foundational aeronautical knowledge remains load-bearing scaffolding for every certificated-pilot course and for the safe operation the flight labs certify, and a pilot must retain this understanding to verify automated outputs where errors carry safety consequences. The rating holds Medium, explicitly capped by foundational role from reaching High. The uncertainty is pedagogical — how ground knowledge is taught when AI supplies the computation — not whether aeronautical fundamentals remain instrumentally necessary for students continuing toward certification, which in the central case they clearly do. In practice the flight labs will not certify a pilot who cannot reason aeronautically, so the ground substrate endures even as the arithmetic is offloaded to software.
AES 1100.d: Students participate in basic studies in aircraft operation, performance, aerodynamics, and design. Federal aviation regulations and other flight publications needed for private pilot operations are examined. Weather theory and reports and basic flight physiology in the context of flight safety are examined. Skills of air navigation by pilotage, dead reckoning, and the use of fundamental tools of air navigation including radio navigational aids are explored.

r: Aviation Weather teaches atmospheric composition, wind, moisture, stability, turbulence, air masses, fronts, thunderstorms, icing, and fog, and the interpretation of observations, reports, forecasts, and prognostic products. The applied work is fundamentally analytical and interpretive — reading METARs, TAFs, and graphic products and translating them into aviation-relevant meaning — precisely the information-processing tasks task-exposure research associates positively with AI exposure, and automated aviation weather briefing already exists. There is no licensure gate on the course credit. At 24 months the instrumental need is modestly eroded: AI can already parse and summarize weather products competently, though a pilot's real-time safety judgment about go/no-go remains human. As a knowledge course feeding dispatch and flight decisions, its base automatability is Medium at this horizon, with adoption still uneven across the sector.

By 2031, AI will fluently ingest, interpret, and summarize aviation weather data and generate tailored briefings, substantially automating the interpretive tasks this course's knowledge is applied to. The instrumental case erodes toward understanding weather well enough to verify automated products and make safety-critical decisions — a genuine but narrower residue. With no institutional lock and weather interpretation sitting among the more exposed analytical categories, and GDPval showing models nearing expert quality on real deliverables, the rating rises to High. The durable human element is the pilot's or dispatcher's accountable go/no-go judgment, which is exercised in the flight and dispatch courses rather than protected within this knowledge course. Capability trends make the interpretive automation increasingly reliable across this horizon.

A decade out, AI will interpret aviation weather and produce decision-ready briefings with high reliability, and the rationale for a student to master manual product interpretation is largely eroded. The rating holds High. The genuine residue — accountable weather-based safety decisions under uncertainty — remains human, but that judgment lives in operational roles and courses, not in the interpretive knowledge this course delivers, and no accreditation or licensure structure protects the course itself. The uncertainty concerns how much go/no-go authority stays reserved to certificated humans versus decision-support systems, and how fast aviation adopts automated briefing at scale. On the instrumental question, weather interpretation is among the more automatable aviation tasks, and nothing structural holds the rating lower.
AES 1400.d: The student is introduced to the earth's atmospheric composition, temperature, pressure, wind, moisture, and weather stability, turbulence, clouds, air masses, fronts, thunderstorms, icing, fog, and other obstructions to vision. Weather observations, reports, forecasts, and prognoses are interpreted and explained, along with methods for disseminating textual and graphic products.

r: The course is FAA pilot training under 14 CFR Part 61 or 141 toward a Private Pilot Certificate, with credit contingent on the student actually obtaining the airman certificate. The applied task is physically operating an aircraft and demonstrating airman competency to a Designated Pilot Examiner — an embodied, safety-critical, federally regulated activity. Task-exposure frameworks place real-time vehicle operation among the least automatable categories, and the FAA certification standard is a hard external mandate no model displaces. Autoflight and advanced avionics already exist and are irrelevant to the requirement that a certificated private pilot demonstrate manual competency. The binding constraint is doubled here: embodiment and a licensure gate that makes the certificate itself the deliverable. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact; the regulatory floor alone forecloses any erosion.

Continued advances in autonomy and flight-deck automation will not alter the FAA's airman-certification framework within five years; safety regulation in aviation is deliberate and slow, and diffusion of certified autonomy into general-aviation primary training is negligible on this horizon. The verification burden is definitional — a pilot certificate attests that a human can safely operate the aircraft, including when automation fails, exactly the adversarial, non-obvious-failure condition the jagged-frontier evidence shows keeps human competence necessary. The course's instrumental necessity is preserved by embodiment and by one of the firmest institutional locks in the catalog. Nothing in the capability trajectory reaches the binding constraint. The rating stays Low with high confidence. Autoflight capability already exceeds what a private certificate requires and remains beside the point; the credential attests to the human, not the machine.

By 2036 uncrewed and highly automated flight will be materially more capable, and one can imagine regulatory movement on commercial autonomy. But the private-pilot certificate this lab builds toward rests on demonstrated human airmanship, and there is no credible central-case path to the FAA eliminating that requirement within the decade. The embodied psychomotor skill and real-time judgment are not the kind of task AI substitutes; they are the kind it is trusted to assist. The rating holds Low; the wide-uncertainty caveat applies to the aviation labor market broadly, not to whether a student still needs to learn to fly. Both embodiment and licensure keep the instrumental case firmly intact. The instrumental question is not whether aircraft can fly themselves but whether a student must still demonstrate airmanship to be certificated, and the answer stays yes.
AES 1500.d: Students engage in Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) pilot training under Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 61 or Part 141 towards a Private Pilot Certificate. Students receive course credit after obtaining the FAA Private Pilot Certificate.

r: This simulation lab develops instrument attitude flying — scanning, interpreting, and controlling — in a flight training device using conventional and advanced flight decks, together with radio navigation across ground- and satellite-based systems. Although conducted in a device rather than an aircraft, the graded competence is embodied and real-time: the psychomotor instrument scan and control inputs a pilot must internalize. Task-exposure research places such real-time control among the least automatable categories. The binding constraint is FAA certification: simulator training under an approved Part 141 curriculum counts toward the instrument rating, so the lab feeds a licensure-gated credential no model obtains on the student's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need to build instrument flying skill is fully intact; automation flying the approach does not substitute for the pilot learning to fly it.

By 2031, flight-training devices and automation will be more sophisticated, and AI may enhance debriefing and scenario generation. None of that reaches the core: a pilot developing the instrument scan and control competence required to fly safely in instrument meteorological conditions, including when automation degrades. The verification burden is safety-critical and the failure modes non-obvious — spatial disorientation and misinterpreted instruments are lethal — which the jagged-frontier evidence ties directly to durable human competence. FAA airman-certification requirements, into which this simulator time feeds, do not restructure within five years. The instrumental case is held by embodiment, verification burden, and licensure together. The rating stays Low. Simulator time only counts because it builds transferable human skill; a device flying itself defeats the purpose of the training the FAA credits toward the rating.

A decade out, autoflight and even single-pilot automation concepts will be more capable, and one can imagine regulatory evolution around automated operations. Even so, instrument-rating training rests on demonstrated human instrument competence, and there is no credible central-case path to the FAA removing that demonstrated skill requirement by 2036. The specific competence this lab builds — real-time instrument scan, interpretation, and control — is the kind AI assists, not the kind it performs for the learner. The rating holds Low, anchored by the embodied-simulation core and the certification lock. The genuine uncertainty concerns the future shape of the pilot's role under heavier automation, not whether an instrument student still needs to fly the scan.
AES 1710.d: Students in the course learn basic flight instruments, radio navigation, aviation weather, aircraft performance, weight and balance, and aeronautical decision-making. The fundamentals of instrument attitude flight (scanning, interpreting, and controlling) are practiced in a flight training device utilizing conventional and advanced flight deck systems. Radio navigation is introduced and includes both ground-based and satellite-based systems.

r: This survey introduces the aviation and aerospace industry — key organizations, competitive and global dynamics, emerging technology, and demographic factors — with field visits used to observe and analyze organizational activities. The applied tasks are informational and analytical: gathering industry information, characterizing organizations, and producing analysis of sector dynamics. Observed-usage data shows such writing and office-analysis tasks are heavily represented in AI use, and GDPval indicates models approach expert quality on comparable deliverables. No accreditation or licensure gates the course. At 24 months the instrumental need is modestly eroded — AI can compile and analyze industry information competently — though the field-visit experiential component and a student's own developing sector literacy retain value, and adoption remains uneven. Rating Medium, reflecting a survey knowledge course.

By 2031, AI will fluently research, structure, and draft industry analyses of the aviation and aerospace sector, automating most of the analytical execution the course teaches. The instrumental case shifts toward directing and verifying AI-generated analysis and toward the experiential learning of site visits, but with no institutional lock nothing caps the erosion at the course level. Industry analysis sits among the exposed office-and-analysis categories the evidence flags positively for exposure. The rating rises to High. The durable residue — judgment about which sources and framings matter, and firsthand observation from field visits — is real but does not by itself hold a knowledge survey at Low across this horizon.

A decade out, AI competently performs industry research and analysis end-to-end, and the rationale for a student to produce sector analyses as a course output is largely eroded. The rating holds High. The genuine residue is experiential and judgmental — what one learns from being physically present at an aerospace organization and from evaluating conflicting analyses — but that is a small share of the course, and no institutional structure protects it. The uncertainty concerns how much analytical judgment stays human versus delegated to AI, and diffusion could lag. On the instrumental question, industry exploration and analysis is among the more automatable knowledge tasks, and nothing structural holds the rating lower in the central case.
AES 1910.d: Students will be introduced to the aviation and aerospace industry, including an overview of key organizations and dynamics that shape the industry. Given availability of organizations, students will perform field visits to participate in tours and analyze the types of activities performed. Industry factors such as emerging technology, competition, globalization, and demographic diversification will also be discussed.

r: This one-credit course introduces analytical tools to quantify aerospace performance parameters and system properties, plus the fundamental metrics used across aircraft and satellite operations — foundational computation for downstream industry analysis. The applied tasks are quantitative: computing performance parameters, applying operational metrics, and processing data. Observed-usage data identifies Computer and Mathematical work as the single largest AI-use category, and task-exposure research places quantitative analysts among the most-exposed occupations. There is no institutional lock. At 24 months the instrumental need is partly eroded — AI and even prior software readily perform these calculations — but the course builds early quantitative fluency that scaffolds the Analysis II and III sequence, and a student still needs to understand the metrics to use tools well. Rating Medium at this horizon.

By 2031, AI will fluently execute the performance calculations and metric computations this course teaches, and the doubling capability trend suggests reliable automation of exactly this quantitative work. The instrumental case erodes toward conceptual fluency needed to specify and verify computed results, but as an introductory building block rather than deep scaffolding for a whole major, the cap is weak. Quantitative-analysis tasks are among the most exposed in the entire evidence base, and productivity studies show large speedups on computational work. The rating rises to High. The residue — understanding what a parameter means well enough to catch an implausible result — is genuine but does not hold a computation-centric one-credit course at Low.

A decade out, symbolic and numerical computation of aerospace performance parameters is trivial for AI and has been for years, and the rationale for a student to execute these calculations is largely eroded. The rating holds High. The durable human element is quantitative judgment — knowing which metric to apply and recognizing a wrong answer — but that is exercised more in downstream analysis than in this introductory tool course, and no institutional structure protects it. The uncertainty is pedagogical: how much hand computation a quantitatively literate aerospace analyst needs when tools are ubiquitous. On the instrumental question, this is among the most automatable content in the batch, and nothing structural holds it lower.
AES 1920.d: Students are introduced to analytical tools used in aerospace science to quantify performance parameters and properties of systems properties which form the foundation of industry analysis. Additional emphasis is placed on fundamental metrics used during aerospace operations, ranging from aircraft to satellite applications.

r: This one-credit course extends the analysis sequence to mission profiles, teaching how flight trajectories are determined and how aerodynamic forces influence them, and how aerospace data is formatted and presented. The applied tasks are quantitative and computational: trajectory determination, aerodynamic-force calculation, and data formatting. Observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical work is the largest AI-use category, and task-exposure research ranks quantitative analysts among the most exposed. No institutional lock applies. At 24 months the instrumental need is partly eroded — trajectory and force computations are the kind AI and existing tools perform readily — but the course scaffolds the visualization work of Analysis III and builds fluency a student needs to interpret results. Rating Medium at this horizon, reflecting a computational building-block course.

By 2031, AI will reliably compute mission profiles, trajectories, and aerodynamic-force relationships and format the associated data, automating the bulk of what this course's knowledge is applied to. The capability trend of rapidly lengthening task horizons points to dependable automation of exactly this bounded quantitative work. The instrumental case erodes toward specifying problems and verifying outputs; as a small building-block course its scaffolding cap is weak, and quantitative analysis is among the most exposed categories in the evidence. The rating rises to High. The residue — recognizing a physically implausible trajectory result — is real but does not hold a computation-centric course at Low across this horizon. Observed usage confirms mathematical work is the most represented AI-use category, so the automation pressure on exactly this content is direct rather than speculative.

A decade out, trajectory and aerodynamic computation is routine for AI, and the rationale for a student to execute it by hand is largely eroded. The rating holds High. The durable human element is physical judgment about whether a computed mission profile makes sense, but that judgment is exercised across applied contexts more than in this introductory tool course, and nothing institutional protects it. The uncertainty is pedagogical — how much manual computation aerospace analysts need when solvers are ubiquitous — rather than about whether the tasks automate. On the rating's own question, this content is among the most automatable in the batch, and no structural brake holds it lower in the central case.
AES 1930.d: Students are introduced to analytical tools used in aerospace science to determine mission profiles used in industry applications. Additional emphasis is placed on flight trajectories and how they are influenced by aerodynamic forces. Furthermore, students explore how aerospace data is presented and how analytical tools are used to format data.

By 2031, AI will fluently compute aerodynamic maneuver parameters and generate mission-profile and radar visualizations, automating most of the course's applied work; code-assisted plotting is already a strong-productivity domain. The instrumental case erodes toward interpreting and verifying AI-generated visuals, and as a terminal course nothing caps that erosion. Quantitative and visualization tasks sit among the most exposed categories in the evidence base. The rating rises to High. The residue — reading a trajectory plot critically and catching a misrendered maneuver — is genuine but does not hold a computation-and-visualization course at Low, particularly with no scaffolding or institutional protection to lean on across this horizon. Observed usage places mathematical and computer work at the top of the AI-use distribution, making the automation of this plotting and calculation content immediate rather than distant.

A decade out, computing and visualizing aerospace mission profiles is routine for AI, and the rationale for a student to produce these artifacts is largely eroded. The rating holds High. The durable element is interpretive judgment about whether a visualization faithfully represents the underlying dynamics, but that is a thin residue and nothing institutional protects the course. The uncertainty is pedagogical rather than substantive — how visualization is taught when tools generate it instantly. On the instrumental question, this content is among the most automatable in the batch, and no structural brake holds the rating lower in the central case; the analysis sequence overall trends strongly toward automation. The analysis sequence as a whole is among the most exposed content in the batch, and this terminal visualization course carries neither scaffolding nor a transfer mandate to slow the shift.
AES 1940.d: Students are introduced to analytical tools used in aerospace science to visually depict mission profiles used in industry applications. Additional emphasis are placed on the visualization of flight trajectories, vectoring, and radar activities. Furthermore, students calculate aerodynamic maneuvers and parameters for various phases of a mission life cycle.

This is exactly the office-and-business analytical category the evidence flags as exposed. The rating rises to High. The residue — accountable judgment about which transformation investments make sense in a specific aerospace operation — is real but is exercised in practice and management roles, not protected within this knowledge course across the horizon. GDPval's finding that models near expert quality on real deliverables applies squarely to the process-mapping and strategy write-ups this course produces, reinforcing the upward move.

On the instrumental question, this analytical content trends strongly toward automation, and nothing structural holds the rating lower in the central case. AES 1950.d: Students are introduced to the concepts of digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation, as well as enabling technologies and business processes, including the fourth industrial revolution in the aviation and space sectors of the aerospace industry. This course specifically focuses on the application of those concepts, technologies, and processes from the aerospace supply chain and manufacturing perspectives.

Diffusion may lag capability, and organizational inertia could slow adoption, but neither is an institutional brake on the course, and the analytical work itself trends toward automation.
AES 1960.d: Students explore workforce development within various sectors and operations of the global aerospace industry. An analysis of historical workforce trends and contemporary barriers impacting career development and organizational effectiveness provides insight into the aerospace industry. Key topics include hiring practices, access to technology, and global collaboration to emphasize the strategic importance of innovation and leadership within the aerospace workforce. Students gain insights into how systemic factors shape workforce dynamics and learn to develop actionable solutions to enhance career pathways.

r: Unlike the introductory UAS knowledge course, this is an applied flight-and-control course with onsite and field-trip practicum: principles of flight, mission planning, systems control, crew resource management, and hands-on operation of UAV vehicles with emphasis on operational safety. The core graded competence is partly embodied — real-time control of the vehicle and coordinated crew operation in the field — which task-exposure research places among the lower-exposure real-time and manual categories. Verification burden is meaningful: an operational error in the field has physical-safety consequences and non-obvious failure modes, the jagged-frontier condition. Although drones are increasingly autonomous, the practicum builds the human operator's control and CRM judgment. At 24 months, with the embodied practicum protective, the instrumental need is not eroded. Rating Low.

By 2031, UAV autonomy will be markedly more capable and will automate more routine flight and mission execution. But this course's applied core — the operator's real-time control, field decision-making, and crew coordination under safety constraints — remains partly embodied and verification-heavy, and diffusion of full autonomy into supervised training and field operations lags capability. The mission-planning and regulatory portions are exposed, but the hands-on control and CRM competence is the protective residue. The rating stays Low across this horizon: even as drones fly themselves more, a human operator trained to supervise, intervene, and manage crew safety remains necessary, and the embodied practicum is not a task AI performs for the learner.

A decade out, UAV operations will be substantially autonomous in many settings, and more of the flight and mission execution this course covers will be performed by the systems themselves, pushing base automatability up. The embodied and verification-heavy core — a human operator's real-time control and safety judgment when autonomy degrades — resists full substitution and keeps the rating from rising past Medium. But with no licensure or accreditation lock on the course and genuine encroachment of autonomy on hands-on control tasks, the protective margin narrows; the rating moves to Medium at 2036. The honest uncertainty is how much supervised human control persists in regulated field operations versus giving way to certified autonomy.
AES 2040.d: Students will be introduced to the principles of flight and control as applied to unmanned aeronautical vehicles (UAVs). Students will receive class lecture plus onsite and field trip learning experiences as applied to the flight and control of UAV vehicles. Topics include principles of flight, mission planning, systems control, and safety of personnel, safety in the operational environment, compliance with regulations and procedures. Human factors analysis with focus on crew resource management is also introduced. Opportunities for applied practicum, including field trip work setting activities are provided.

r: This history course examines how individuals and defining events shaped aviation and aerospace — propulsion, structural materials, navigation, high-altitude and spaceflight — and analyzes historical developments for their relevance to future opportunities. The applied tasks are reading, synthesis, interpretation, and historical writing, which observed-usage data shows are prominent AI-use categories and which task-exposure research associates positively with exposure; models generate fluent historical narrative and analysis, and GDPval shows near-expert quality on comparable deliverables. It is a terminal survey with no institutional lock and little downstream scaffolding. At 24 months the instrumental need is modestly eroded — AI competently produces historical synthesis — but a student's own interpretive and evidentiary reasoning retains value, and the course's base automatability sits at Medium. Rating Medium at this horizon.

By 2031, AI will fluently research, synthesize, and write aviation and aerospace history, automating essentially the whole of what this course's knowledge is applied to. The instrumental case erodes toward the student's own capacity to interpret evidence and construct historical arguments — a genuine residue — but as a terminal course with no scaffolding role and no general-education or licensure lock, nothing caps the erosion. Historical writing and synthesis are among the exposed, positively-associated task categories. The rating rises to High. The durable human element, discerning a sound historical interpretation from a fluent but shallow one, matters, yet it does not by itself hold an unprotected history survey at Low across this horizon.

A decade out, AI produces sophisticated historical narrative and analysis of aviation and aerospace on demand, and the rationale for a student to generate such writing as coursework is substantially eroded. The rating holds High. The durable residue is critical historical judgment — evaluating sources and interpretations rather than accepting fluent output — but that is a narrow protection for an unmandated terminal course. The uncertainty concerns how history is taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI, not whether the writing-and-synthesis tasks automate. On the instrumental question, this content trends strongly toward automation, and with no scaffolding or institutional lock, nothing structural holds the rating lower in the central case. Observed usage confirms writing and synthesis are prominent AI-use categories, so the automation pressure on this history survey is direct, and no mandate exists to hold it lower.
AES 2050.d: Students examine how individuals and defining events of the past influenced the development of aviation and aerospace science. From early myths to advents in aerospace science, such as advances in propulsion systems, structural materials, navigation techniques, high altitude flights, and weather analysis have had upon the progress of manned flight in and beyond the atmosphere are considered. Students vicariously relive many of the extraordinary experiences of early aviators and space pioneers. The evolution of aviation science in comparison to aerospace science is described. Historical events are analyzed for applicability to embracing future opportunities and career paths in aviation and space science.

r: Instrument Pilot Ground is the knowledge course for instrument flight: instrument flight-control technique, radio navigation, federal aviation regulations, air traffic control procedures, avionics systems, and IMC weather. The applied tasks are informational and analytical — regulatory interpretation, procedure knowledge, avionics and navigation reasoning — sitting among the more AI-exposed categories, with models handling regulatory and procedural explanation competently and GDPval showing near-expert quality on comparable deliverables. Unlike Private Pilot Ground, its scaffolding is narrower, and no licensure gates the course credit itself. At 24 months the instrumental need is modestly eroded: AI can explain instrument procedures and regulations on demand, but the course grounds the aeronautical knowledge a pilot applies in the instrument-rating flight training. Rating Medium at this horizon.

By 2031, AI will fluently deliver and tutor instrument-flight knowledge — procedures, regulations, avionics, and IMC weather — automating most of the informational work this course's knowledge is applied to, with capability trends pointing to reliable coverage of this bounded material. The instrumental case erodes toward the conceptual fluency a pilot needs to fly instruments and verify automated systems; its modest scaffolding role caps the erosion only weakly, and no licensure locks the course credit. The rating rises to High. The durable residue is the pilot's applied judgment in actual instrument flight, but that competence is built and certified in the flight labs, not protected within this knowledge course. GDPval showing near-expert quality on comparable deliverables applies to the procedural and regulatory explanations at the heart of this ground course, reinforcing the upward move.

A decade out, AI competently supplies instrument-flight knowledge — procedures, regulations, avionics, weather — and the rationale for a student to master this material as a standalone ground course is largely eroded. The rating holds High. The durable human element is the applied instrument-flying competence certified in the labs, not the ground knowledge itself, and no institutional structure protects this course. The uncertainty concerns how ground instruction restructures once AI supplies the knowledge, and how instrument-rating requirements evolve. On the instrumental question, instrument ground knowledge is among the more automatable aviation content, and with only weak scaffolding and no lock, nothing structural holds the rating lower in the central case.
AES 2120.d: Students participate in a comprehensive exploration of instrument flight, focusing on the principles and techniques required for safe and efficient operations in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). Students engage in a detailed study of instrument flight control techniques, radio navigation, and instrument flight operations. Students thoroughly analyze federal aviation regulations (FARs) and air traffic control (ATC) procedures related to instrument flight. Additionally, students examine avionics systems and navigational aids essential for instrument operations and review weather information specific to instrument flight.

r: This course introduces air traffic services — procedures, communications, regulations, emergencies, and airspace — with heavy hands-on radar simulation: aircraft separation, identification, speed control, flight-progress-strip usage, and emergency handling. The applied competence is real-time, high-stakes, and interpersonal: monitoring traffic and issuing control instructions under time pressure, an activity task-exposure research places among the low-exposure real-time and interactive categories. Verification burden is extreme — a separation error is potentially catastrophic and its failure non-obvious, exactly the jagged-frontier condition — and the FAA's controller-training and safety regime is deliberate and slow to change. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: automation may assist controllers, but the real-time separation judgment the simulator lab builds is not a task AI performs on the student's behalf. Rating Low.

By 2031, ATC decision-support and automation tools will be more capable, assisting with conflict detection and sequencing. But the core competence — real-time traffic separation, live pilot communication, and emergency judgment — remains a high-presence, high-verification human task, and the failure cost is catastrophic, keeping a knowledgeable human necessary. FAA adoption of consequential ATC automation is exceptionally slow and safety-gated, so diffusion lags capability sharply on this horizon. The instrumental case is held by real-time interpersonal presence and verification burden together. The rating stays Low: the simulator lab builds exactly the real-time controlling and communicating competence that resists substitution, and nothing in the capability trajectory reaches that binding constraint within five years.

A decade out, ATC automation research may mature and more traffic-management functions could be machine-assisted, raising base automatability somewhat. Even so, the human core this course builds — real-time separation judgment, live communication, and emergency decision-making under catastrophic error cost — remains necessary in the central case through 2036, both because verification demands do not disappear and because the FAA's safety-critical adoption of autonomy is glacial. The dampening effect of real-time presence and verification holds the rating at Low. The genuine uncertainty is how much routine sequencing automates around a still-human controlling core, not whether a student pursuing ATC still needs the real-time competence; heavier automation raises the premium on controllers who can judge when an automated instruction is unsafe.
AES 2200.d: This course is an introduction to air traffic services, procedures, communications, record keeping, regulations, emergencies, and air space constructions. Basic and advanced ATC (air traffic control) radar topics are introduced with emphasis on hands-on application in the simulator lab. Lab exercises encompass aircraft separation, identification and speed control, flight progress strip usage, emergency procedures, and the elements necessary for the safe operation of the ATC system.

r: This course prepares students to work as flight dispatchers: operational regulations, decision-making, safety, weather-based dispatch judgment, and load planning. The applied tasks — flight planning, load and balance computation, weather-driven dispatch decisions, and compliance checking — are substantially computational and are already supported by airline dispatch software, so observed-usage patterns in mathematical and office work suggest meaningful exposure. But the dispatcher shares operational control with the captain, making the decisions safety-critical with non-obvious failure modes — a genuine verification burden that dampens automatability — and the FAA aircraft-dispatcher certification pathway is a contributory institutional constraint. At 24 months the verification-heavy, safety-critical nature holds the instrumental need largely intact: AI can compute a load plan, but accountable dispatch judgment remains human. Rating Low at this horizon.

By 2031, AI will more fully automate flight planning, load-and-balance computation, and weather-based routing, materially reducing the routine execution this course teaches. The instrumental case erodes, but the verification burden caps it: a dispatcher's decisions carry joint operational responsibility and catastrophic error potential, so the human who understands the computation must validate it — the jagged-frontier caution applied to a safety-critical role. The FAA dispatcher-certification pathway persists and slows any structural change. The rating rises to Medium rather than High: the computational tasks are increasingly automatable, but accountable, certificated dispatch judgment and the licensure pathway keep the knowledge instrumentally necessary across this horizon. Airlines already lean heavily on dispatch software, so the capability is not hypothetical; what holds the rating at Medium is accountable, certificated human judgment rather than any gap in the tools.

A decade out, AI competently performs most dispatch computation — planning, load balancing, and weather routing — and the execution rationale is substantially eroded. But dispatch is a safety-critical function with shared operational control and severe, non-obvious failure modes, so verifying and owning the automated recommendation remains a trained human responsibility, and the FAA certification regime for dispatchers changes slowly. The rating holds Medium, capped from High by verification burden and the licensure pathway. The genuine uncertainty is how much accountable dispatch authority stays reserved to certificated humans versus delegated to validated automation; regulatory conservatism in aviation safety favors the human remaining in the loop through 2036. Aviation's conservative safety culture makes wholesale removal of the human dispatcher improbable within the decade, even as the underlying computation becomes fully automatable.
AES 2220.d: Students are introduced to the topics needed to prepare them to work as a flight dispatcher. Regulations required for operations are a vital area of knowledge and will be covered. Students examine the methods of decision-making, safety, and weather conditions related to dispatch decisions.

r: As the first Flight Team course, this prepares students for National Intercollegiate Flying Association meets through flight and ground accuracy and timed events, and is required of new Precision Flight Team members. The applied competence is embodied precision airmanship — hand-flying accuracy landings and navigation events under competition conditions — plus ground events. Task-exposure research places real-time vehicle operation among the least automatable categories, alongside manual and physical work negatively associated with exposure. Generating a competition strategy is trivial for a model; flying a power-off precision landing to a spot is not a task AI performs for the student. Embodiment is the binding constraint. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop this psychomotor precision-flying skill is wholly intact; there is no route by which automation substitutes for the pilot learning to fly the events.

By 2031, flight automation will be more capable, and analysis tools may support competition preparation. None of that reaches the core: a pilot developing precision hand-flying and real-time judgment for accuracy and timed events. The verification burden is safety-critical and the failure modes immediate — a botched precision maneuver is physically dangerous — the adversarial, non-obvious condition the jagged-frontier evidence ties to durable human competence. Diffusion of autonomy into hand-flown collegiate competition flying is negligible, and adoption of AI in physical-skill acquisition lags capability broadly. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment. The rating stays Low: no model performs the precision flying the course builds, and nothing in the trajectory reaches that constraint within five years.

By 2036 highly automated flight will be materially more capable, but the specific competence this course develops — a human pilot's embodied precision control and real-time judgment in accuracy and timed events — is not a task AI executes on the student's behalf; embodiment is the entire point. The most plausible decade-scale change is in preparation and analysis tools, not in whether learning to fly precision events requires doing it. Task-exposure frameworks keep real-time vehicle operation and physical skill among the most durable human categories. The rating holds Low; the honest caveat concerns the broader aviation labor market, not the instrumental necessity of embodied precision-flight training, which remains intact under any credible central case through 2036.
AES 2330.d: The first Flight Team course prepares students for participation in the National Intercollegiate Flying Association regional and national flying meets. Flight and ground event accuracy and time events are learned. This course is required for students who are new members of the MSU Denver Precision Flight Team.

r: The applied work is physically flying aerobatic and glider maneuvers with precision, accuracy, and timing for International Aerobatic Club collegiate competition, real-time psychomotor aircraft control under high-G, unforgiving conditions. These map to O*NET activities dominated by operating vehicles and controlling machines in real time, which task-exposure research consistently places among the least automatable categories, alongside other manual and physical work. No language or reasoning model performs an aileron roll or a coordinated glider approach on a student's behalf; the competence is embodied and cultivated only by doing. Autonomous flight exists but is irrelevant to whether a team member can personally execute competition maneuvers judged on human precision. At 24 months the instrumental need is untouched, embodiment, not adoption timing, is the operative variable, and the error tolerance in aerobatics keeps a trained human indispensable.

By 2031, drone autonomy and flight automation will be markedly more capable, but neither reaches the specific competence this course builds: a student's own aerobatic and glider airmanship, demonstrated live in IAC collegiate events. The activity is defined by real-time embodied control and split-second judgment under aerodynamic loads that task-exposure frameworks classify as low-exposure precisely because they are physical and non-digital. Verification is definitional here, competition scoring rewards demonstrated human precision, and a maneuver either is or is not flown cleanly by the pilot. There is no institutional shortcut and no automation substitute for cultivating the skill. The most plausible five-year change is better simulation for practice, not any erosion of the need to fly the maneuvers oneself. The rating stays Low; embodiment holds firmly across this horizon.

A decade out, autonomous aerobatic drones may be impressive, and the broader aviation labor market faces genuine uncertainty. But the instrumental question, whether a student on the Aerobatic and Glider Team still needs to develop personal maneuvering skill, is essentially unchanged, because the course exists to build embodied human airmanship for live competition, not to produce an output a model could generate. The psychomotor and real-time judgment sit in the categories task-exposure research finds durably resistant to automation. The honest hedge concerns how the sport and its training evolve, not whether flying the aircraft remains a human act. Rating holds Low with high confidence; embodiment is the whole point, and nothing in the capability trajectory reaches it by 2036.
AES 2350.d: The first Aerobatic and Glider Course prepares students for participation in the International Aerobatic Club (IAC) Collegiate Program, national team and individual collegiate events. Aerobatic flight maneuvers, precision, accuracy and timed events are learned. Required for all students who are members of the MSU Denver Aerobatic and Glider Team.

r: This lab is FAA flight training under 14 CFR Part 61/141 toward an Instrument Rating, with course credit contingent on the student actually earning the FAA certificate. The applied task is physically operating an aircraft solely by reference to instruments and demonstrating airman competency to an examiner, an embodied, safety-critical, federally regulated activity. Task-exposure research places real-time vehicle operation among the least automatable categories, and the FAA certification standard is a hard external mandate that no AI capability displaces. Advanced avionics and autoflight already exist and are beside the point: the requirement is that a certificated instrument pilot can personally fly approaches, holds, and unusual attitudes when automation fails. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact; the regulatory floor alone forecloses any erosion, and the credit-equals-certificate structure makes the lock absolute.

Continued advances in flight-deck autonomy will not alter the FAA's airman certification framework within five years, regulatory change in aviation safety is deliberate and slow, and diffusion of certified autonomy into general-aviation instrument training is negligible on this horizon. The verification burden is definitional: an instrument rating attests that a human can safely operate in instrument meteorological conditions, including when systems degrade, exactly the adversarial, non-obvious-failure condition that keeps embodied human competence necessary. The lab's credit remains gated on the FAA certificate, so no capability trajectory reaches the binding constraint. The rating stays Low; the jagged-frontier evidence, that users outside AI's competence range trust it wrongly, only sharpens why a pilot must be able to fly the approach unaided. Nothing here erodes at 2031.

By 2036 highly automated flight will be materially more capable, and one can imagine regulatory movement on commercial autonomy. But the instrument rating this lab builds toward rests on demonstrated human airmanship, and there is no credible central-case path to the FAA eliminating that requirement within the decade. The embodied psychomotor skill and real-time decision-making are not the kind of task AI substitutes; they are the kind it is trusted to assist under human command. The rating holds Low; the wide-uncertainty caveat applies to the aviation labor market broadly, how many pilots, flying what, not to whether a student still needs to learn to fly on instruments and pass the checkride. Embodiment plus licensure remain among the firmest locks in the catalog.
AES 2500.d: Students engage in Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) pilot training under Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 61 or Part 141 towards an Instrument Rating. Students receive course credit after obtaining the FAA Instrument Rating.

r: The applied work is operating space-mission modeling and visualization software, AGI's Systems Tool Kit and A.I. Solutions' FreeFlyer, to perform orbital-mechanics analysis, learning software interfaces and space-mission applications. These map to O*NET activities of interacting with computers and analyzing information, and observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical work is the single largest AI usage category. AI agents increasingly drive technical software and generate and interpret analytical outputs, so the raw tasks carry real exposure. But at 24 months adoption of agentic control over specialized aerospace tools like STK is thin, and this introductory course is prerequisite scaffolding for higher-level modeling coursework such as AES 3607. Orbital mechanics also carries a verification concern, a wrong ephemeris is not obviously wrong. The realized erosion within two years is partial; the rating is Medium, held down by the course's foundational role in the simulation sequence.

By 2031, AI systems will more competently operate modeling environments and produce orbital analyses, and GDPval-style evidence of models approaching expert performance on real deliverables suggests the analytical output this course teaches becomes broadly automatable. The foundational cap binds only at the near-term horizon, so it no longer holds the rating down at five years. Absent embodiment, licensure, or a strong verification barrier specific to introductory tool use, little preserves the instrumental case for a student personally learning STK interfaces when an agent can drive them. The residual is judgment about whether a simulation's setup and assumptions are physically sensible, real, but narrower than the course's interface-focused content. The rating rises to High, with the hedge that specialized aerospace-software adoption may lag the general capability trend.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently operating mission-modeling software and generating orbital analyses with limited human input, and the applied tasks this introductory course teaches are substantially performed by capable systems. With no embodiment, no licensure, and only a near-term foundational cap, little protects the instrumental necessity of a student learning these interfaces by hand. The capability trend, task horizons doubling every few months on the METR read, points toward tool operation being handled end-to-end. The rating is High, hedged by ten-year forecasting uncertainty and by the possibility that verifying physically sound mission models retains a human premium held by fewer, more expert practitioners. The intrinsic value of understanding orbital mechanics is real and separate from this instrumental reading.
AES 2607.d: This class will provide a fundamental introduction to Orbital Mechanics and Physics software modeling. The student will learn the interfaces of various Space Mission Modeler and Visualization software products, such as AGI's System Tool Kit (STK) and A.I. Solutions' Freeflyer as applied in Orbital Mechanics. This class will offer a foundation for higher level coursework on Space Mission Modeler and Visualization software with a sophisticated focus on software interface and space mission applications. Students are provided with necessary software licensing with course enrollment.

r: The applied work is real-time spacecraft operation: generating daily mission plans, conducting real-time command and control in a Mission Operations Center, and performing post-pass data analysis using an interactive spacecraft simulator. These map to O*NET activities of controlling machines and processes, monitoring, and decision-making under time pressure. Ground-operations automation is advancing, and observed-usage data documents substantial automation of routine analytical tasks, but the binding factor here is verification burden: an erroneous real-time command can be catastrophic and its failure mode non-obvious, exactly the adversarial condition that keeps a knowledgeable human operator necessary. At 24 months, with thin diffusion of autonomous ground systems into training contexts, the realized erosion is minimal; the course develops the operator judgment that anomaly response demands. The rating is Low, protected by the safety-critical verification burden inherent in flying a real mission.

By 2031, autonomous ground-station software and AI-assisted planning will handle much of the routine command sequencing, scheduling, and pass-data reduction this course teaches, and Census diffusion data suggests adoption will spread unevenly but genuinely across operations settings. Yet the verification burden does not lift: the jagged-frontier evidence, that operators outside AI's reliable range mis-trust its outputs, is acute where a mistaken command loses a spacecraft. Real-time anomaly judgment during a live pass keeps a trained human in the loop. The rating stays Low: routine planning automates, but the operator competence for non-nominal situations remains necessary, and the role shifts toward supervising automated operations rather than being replaced by them. Diffusion into the specific real-time-ops training context is still maturing at this horizon.

A decade out, much routine spacecraft operation, planning, nominal command and control, pass analysis, is plausibly automated end-to-end, and the operator role concentrates on anomaly response, oversight, and contingency judgment. The instrumental case for learning nominal operations erodes, so the rating rises to Medium at 2036. But the safety-critical verification demand, where failures are catastrophic and non-obvious, sustains a residual need for humans who understand what the automated system is doing well enough to intervene. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the real-time-judgment core automates versus how much stays human under a still-conservative space-safety culture. Rating is Medium, not High: the administrative shell of operations automates around a still-human contingency core, and no capability read cleanly removes the operator from the loop.
AES 2630.d: Provides the student with an overview of the real-time skills, techniques, and methods necessary to conduct a space mission as a Spacecraft Operator including generation of the daily planning and successful execution of the real-time portion of a space mission. The differences in ground and space system architectures, mission dynamics (orbit, spacecraft agility, etc.), operations tempo, and the planning timeline inherent in various types of missions are examined. The laboratory includes hands-on exercises in the AES Mission Operations Center to create a daily mission plan, conduct spacecraft real-time command and control, and perform post contact (pass) data analysis. A real-time ops environment is created using an interactive spacecraft simulator. Focus is on learning the skills necessary to operate a space mission.

r: The applied work is flying a flight training device through instrument procedures, departures, enroute operations, holding patterns, arrivals, and precision and non-precision approaches, under ATC clearances, including normal and abnormal procedures on conventional and advanced flight decks. Though simulated, the competence is embodied and real-time: hands-on aircraft control, scan, and situational awareness that map to O*NET operating and controlling-machines activities, which task-exposure research places outside AI's automatable range. Flight-training-device time in a Part 141 program counts toward the FAA Instrument Rating, tying the course to the federally approved training curriculum. Autoflight can fly an approach, but the course develops the student's own procedural competence for when it cannot. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact, the embodied, real-time psychomotor skill and the FAA training role together foreclose erosion.

By 2031, flight simulation and cockpit automation will be more sophisticated, but the competence this course builds, a pilot's own instrument procedures and real-time situational awareness, including abnormal-procedure handling, is embodied and not delegable to a model. The FAA Part 141 curriculum that gives training-device time its credit value changes on a slow regulatory clock and will not have relaxed within a catalog cycle. Verification is definitional: instrument flight training exists precisely to prepare the human for degraded and abnormal conditions where automation is insufficient. Better AI tutoring may sharpen how students prepare, but it does not fly the procedures for them. The rating stays Low; embodiment and the FAA training framework hold jointly across this horizon, with automation entering as a practice aid rather than a substitute.

A decade out, simulators and flight automation will be far more capable, and the surrounding pilot labor market carries real uncertainty. But the specific thing this course develops, embodied, real-time instrument-flying competence demonstrated in a training device toward an FAA rating, is not a task AI performs on the learner's behalf, and there is no central-case path to the FAA removing simulator-based instrument training from the certification pathway by 2036. The psychomotor and procedural judgment sit in low-exposure categories, and the training-device requirement remains a durable institutional anchor. Rating holds Low; the honest caveat is about how many pilots the industry needs and how much line flying is automated, not about whether learning to fly instruments in a simulator remains instrumentally necessary.
AES 2710.d: Students participate in instrument flight planning, navigation, and situational awareness during departure, enroute, and arrival phases of flight. Simulated flights involve air traffic control (ATC) clearances and FAA instrument procedures, including departures, enroute operations, holding patterns, arrivals, and precision and non-precision approaches. These flights also include normal and abnormal procedures, practiced in a flight training device utilizing conventional and advanced flight deck systems.

r: The applied work is knowledge acquisition and explanation: aircraft nomenclature, design features, and the theory, components, instrumentation, and operation of reciprocating, turboprop, and turbojet engines, plus pressurization, electrical, hydraulic, anti-ice, and pneumatic systems. These map to O*NET activities of getting, processing, and interpreting technical information, the explanatory knowledge work that AI performs fluently. Observed-usage data shows information and writing tasks prominent in AI use, and models already explain engine cycles and system architectures competently. At 24 months, however, adoption in this instructional context is partial, and there is no licensure or embodiment cap; the course is moderately foundational technical background for the aviation sequence. The realized erosion of the instrumental need is partial rather than complete. The rating is Medium: the knowledge is exposed, but two years of diffusion leave the near-term case only partly displaced.

By 2031, AI will competently deliver, tutor, and apply aircraft-systems knowledge on demand, explaining turbomachinery operation, diagnosing conceptual system interactions, and answering technical questions instantly, with GDPval-style evidence pointing to models approaching expert performance on real technical deliverables. Absent embodiment, licensure, or a strong verification barrier specific to this material, little preserves the instrumental case for a student acquiring this knowledge to perform work an assistant handles. The residual is the applied troubleshooting judgment a technician or pilot exercises on real hardware, which this lecture course only partly addresses. The rating rises to High: the systems-and-propulsion knowledge this course transmits is broadly AI-deliverable at this horizon, and no protective constraint caps it. The disciplinary value of understanding aircraft remains real but is intrinsic, outside this rating.

A decade out, AI is an authoritative explainer and applier of aircraft-systems and propulsion knowledge, and the applied tasks this course serves are performed competently with limited human input. With no embodiment, licensure, or foundational cap holding it back, the instrumental case substantially erodes. The rating is High, hedged by ten-year forecasting uncertainty and by the possibility that hands-on maintenance and safety-critical troubleshooting sustain more human systems knowledge than a pure capability read implies, but that embodied residue lives in maintenance labs, not this theory course. Relative to the flight labs in the same program, this knowledge course lacks any embodiment or certification lock, which is exactly why its instrumental necessity is far more exposed by 2036.
AES 3000.d: Students are introduced to aircraft nomenclature, design features, systems, and their components. Students learn the theory, components, instrumentation, and operation of internal combustion, turboprop, and turbojet engines. Additionally, the student learns about pressurization, electrical, hydraulic, anti-ice/de-ice, turbocharging, and pneumatic aircraft systems.

r: The applied work spans acquiring, processing, and analyzing data from photographic, multispectral, infrared, and LiDAR sensors mounted on unmanned aircraft, mission planning, sensor selection, and the data pipeline, with a field practicum for collection. The processing-and-analysis core maps to O*NET analyzing-information and interacting-with-computers activities, and automated photogrammetry and machine-learning classification of multispectral and LiDAR data are precisely where capability is strong; observed-usage data places computational work as the largest AI category. Some tasks remain embodied, flying missions, operating sensors in the field, but the description weights the digital pipeline heavily. At 24 months, adoption of end-to-end automated geospatial processing in this instructional setting is partial, and the field-collection component retains a human role. The realized erosion is partial; the rating is Medium, reflecting substantial but not complete near-term exposure of the analytical core.

By 2031, automated sensor-data processing, orthomosaic generation, spectral classification, LiDAR feature extraction, will be broadly capable and increasingly turnkey, eroding the instrumental rationale for a student to execute the pipeline by hand. Productivity evidence from analogous technical domains shows large speedups when capable tools handle routine processing. What survives is judgment about data quality, mission design, and whether an automated classification is actually correct, a verification concern the jagged-frontier evidence underscores for geospatial inference. But that residue is narrower than the course's processing-and-analysis content, and the field-collection component is a modest fraction. Absent licensure or a strong embodiment cap on the analytical core, the rating rises to High: the data-analysis work this course centers becomes competently automatable at this horizon, with human oversight concentrated on validation.

A decade out, UAS data collection and analysis is substantially automated, autonomous flight planning, onboard processing, and AI interpretation of multispectral and LiDAR products, and the applied analytical tasks this course teaches are performed with limited human input. The rating is High. The hedge is genuine: field data collection retains embodied elements, and verifying that an automated classification would survive scrutiny in a consequential application like surveying or inspection sustains a human premium. The instrumental case erodes as the planning and data-analysis work the course applies to becomes AI-executable. That verification competence keeps a knowledgeable human necessary. The instrumental case for the routine-operations content substantially erodes. But the verification premium in a domain of non-obvious, catastrophic failure modes remains, and the real-time contingency competence the lab develops is where residual human operators concentrate. The rating holds Medium, not High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty about how far autonomy penetrates crewed-mission operations and by the possibility that regulated or high-value missions sustain more human oversight than a pure capability read implies. The direction is clear: routine ops automate around a still-human anomaly-response core.
AES 3630.d: The student gains a deeper understanding of the daily mission planning process, the issues involved with Mission Operations management, and the creation and upkeep of operations documentation and procedures for both routine and contingency system situations. The student also learns about the issues involved in managing the daily interaction of Operations with ground and space support teams (both routine and contingency) for the planning and scheduling of space and ground station assets. The laboratory builds on the student's experience in AES 2630 with increased complexity spacecraft real-time command and control real-time exercises including nominal mission execution and response to spacecraft anomalies. AES 3640.d: Students are introduced to the aerospace systems life cycle to gain a comprehensive understanding of the design and analysis of aerospace systems.
