Rating stays Low; the tools grow more capable while the human management competence remains required.

By 2036, cockpit automation and possible single-pilot autonomy will be materially more capable, and the balance of the course could shift toward higher-order systems management. But real-time management of advanced avionics under instrument conditions - recognizing and correcting automation failures - remains a competence AI assists rather than performs on the pilot's behalf, and its verification premium persists. The rating rises only to Medium, hedged by ten-year uncertainty about how far trusted autonomy penetrates general aviation. AES 3650.d: The course is designed to emphasize advanced instrument procedures, including the use of global positioning system (GPS) and other area navigation (RNAV) systems. FAA-regulated simulator training and the certificated multi-engine pathway do not restructure within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and verification together; rating stays Low. Automation changes what pilots learn to oversee, not whether they must fly the profile themselves.

By 2036, autonomy and simulation fidelity will be markedly greater, and one can imagine more automated multi-engine operations. Even so, the embodied psychomotor skill, real-time emergency judgment, and crew coordination this simulation course builds are not delegable to AI, and the FAA certification framework governing multi-engine training shows no central-case path to removing demonstrated human competence within the decade. The rating holds Low with high confidence. The wide-uncertainty caveat applies to the multi-engine pilot labor market broadly - not to whether a student still needs to learn to manage engine-out flight and CRM, which remains an embodied, safety-critical competence AI assists rather than replaces, and which the certification regime continues to require through the decade.
AES 3710.d: Students are introduced to the fundamentals of multi- engine aircraft systems and aerodynamics, focusing on the unique characteristics of multi-engine operations. Students explore topics such as engine-out aerodynamics and operations, along with normal and emergency procedures. These concepts are applied in a twin- engine simulator, utilizing conventional and advanced flight deck systems. Students examine real-world multi-engine flight scenarios with an emphasis on aeronautical decision-making and crew resource management (CRM).

A decade out, AI is an authoritative, interactive explainer of aviation human factors and physiology, and the instrumental case for a course delivering this knowledge is substantially eroded. But relative to the catalog, this is a clear high-exposure case precisely because nothing - embodiment, licensure, foundational role - holds it back; it tracks the exposed knowledge courses, not the protected flight labs in the same program. The subject's intrinsic value to safe airmanship is real and separate from this instrumental reading, which the rubric does not score.
AES 3850.d: At least junior standing Human factors, physiological effects and problems associated with flight are studied in this course This includes both high- and low-altitude flight environments

r: The course covers aircraft-accident investigation techniques and report writing across operations, air-traffic control, meteorology, witnesses, human factors, cockpit voice and flight-data recorders, structures, powerplants, and maintenance records. Records analysis, FDR/CVR data reduction, and drafting are partly exposed to AI. By 2031, investigative analytics, digital-evidence processing, and report drafting will be more capable and adopted, meaningfully augmenting investigators by surfacing patterns across recorder data and maintenance records. But determining probable cause requires reconciling physical evidence, human factors, and testimony into a defensible finding - adversarial, high-stakes reasoning where a confident wrong conclusion is costly and non-obvious, exactly the jagged-frontier problem. The physical site-and-wreckage examination and witness interviewing remain presence-dependent. The instrumental case is preserved by verification burden and partial embodiment; the role shifts toward directing and validating AI-assisted analysis rather than away from requiring investigative competence. Institutional and evidentiary norms governing what counts as a credible finding change slowly, reinforcing the human role. Rating stays Low across this horizon.

A decade out, AI will absorb much routine analytical work in accident investigation - recorder decoding, data correlation, draft reporting. Yet the human core - embodied evidence examination, interviewing, and courtroom- and inquiry-defensible reasoning about causation - remains necessary in the central case, because the legal and safety-accountability system's verification demands do not disappear and the work is partly physical. The rating holds Low, hedged by uncertainty about how much analysis automates around a still-human investigative core. If anything, heavier automation raises the premium on investigators who can judge when an algorithmic inference would not survive adversarial scrutiny or a formal safety board's review. The uncertainty is in how much of the analytical shell automates around that judgment, not whether the judgment is still required.
AES 3870.d: This course examines techniques and procedures for investigating aircraft accidents/incidents and report writing. Areas of emphasis are operations, air traffic control, meteorology, witnesses, human factors, cockpit voice recorders, structures, power plants, systems, performance, maintenance records, and flight data recorders.

Diffusion of AI into regulatory-analysis and policy work is already visible, and the capability trend points toward broader adoption by this horizon.

A decade out, AI generates authoritative security-policy analysis and historical synthesis on demand, and the instrumental case for a knowledge course in aviation security is substantially eroded. AES 3880.d: The history, development and strategies of prevention and response to aviation security issues are studied in this course. The role of international and national agencies, including statutes and regulations are detailed, with particular emphasis on Transportation Security Regulations as they apply to airports and aircraft operators. The history of air terrorism is addressed, focusing on terrorist threats and governmental responses before and after 9/11/2001.

r: The course examines Normal- and Transport-category aircraft performance and the certification regulations governing it, with students calculating required distances, speeds, and power or thrust settings for flight profiles using performance charts. The jagged-frontier evidence is directly on point: users who over-trust a plausible but wrong performance figure are less accurate than they realize.

A decade out, performance computation is trivial for AI and integrated into flight-planning and dispatch tools, and the execution rationale is largely eroded. But the human ability to sanity-check performance figures where a confident wrong answer risks safety retains real value, and that verification competence is what the course ultimately builds. The rating holds Medium, hedged by ten-year uncertainty and by the possibility that automated flight-planning systems earn enough trust to further reduce human involvement. The direction is clear: the applied calculation automates, while the safety-oriented interpretive judgment persists as the residual competence - insufficient, on its own, to keep the course at Low, but enough to hold it below High.
AES 4040.d: The performance of aircraft from the Normal and Transport categories is examined. Regulations governing the performance requirements of aircraft certification within each category are discussed. Flight profiles are studied, with emphasis on aircraft capabilities and limitations. Required distances, speeds, and power or thrust settings for the various flight conditions are calculated using performance charts.

The instrumental case is preserved by verification burden and partial embodiment together; rating stays Low. The controller's role shifts toward supervising and validating automation, not away from requiring the control competence the simulator builds. Federal certification of controllers, and the deliberate pace of aviation-safety change, reinforce that the competence stays required through this horizon.

A decade out, ATC automation will handle substantially more routine sequencing and conflict resolution, and the balance of the work could shift toward oversight of automated systems. But real-time responsibility for aircraft separation - and for emergencies where an automation failure is instantly catastrophic - keeps a competent human controller necessary in the central case through 2036, and the work stays partly embodied and interpersonal. The rating holds Low, hedged by genuine uncertainty about how far trusted ATC autonomy advances over the decade. The premium on controllers who can recognize and correct an automated system's error, under time pressure, rises rather than disappears. The genuine uncertainty is how much routine sequencing automates around that still-human core, not whether the core competence endures.
AES 4100.d: Introduces advanced ATC radar topics, with emphasis on hands-on application in the simulator lab. Covers aircraft separation; identification and speed control; flight progress strip usage; emergency procedures; and the elements necessary for the safe operation of the ATC system.

r: This course analyzes subsonic and supersonic aerodynamics — airfoil theory, lift and drag calculation, NACA airfoils — and uses a wind-tunnel laboratory to test the Bernoulli equation, Reynolds number, and aerodynamic properties of structures. The wind-tunnel component also remains partly embodied: validating a prediction against physical measurement and diagnosing discrepancies requires the trained human at the bench. These two protective factors cap the erosion at Medium rather than High. The rating rises to Medium: the computational execution is substantially automatable, but the physical experimentation and the safety-critical verification of aerodynamic claims remain instrumentally necessary competencies a model does not perform on the engineer's behalf.

A decade out, AI-driven aerodynamic analysis and generative design will handle most routine computation, and the execution rationale for the coursework is largely eroded. But verifying that an AI-generated aerodynamic design behaves as predicted — reconciling model output with physical reality — remains a necessary human competence where errors carry safety consequences, and the experimental judgment the wind-tunnel work builds is not delegable to a model. The rating holds Medium, capped by verification burden and the residual embodied component from reaching High. The genuine uncertainty is how much physical testing is displaced by high-fidelity simulation versus retained for validation, not whether aerodynamic-reasoning and verification competence is still needed. Even in a heavily automated design environment, someone must judge when a generated airfoil would not survive contact with the air, and that judgment is what the course builds.
